D018-D001_h001.question:
It’s been about three years since the car accident, and I still feel like I’m living in it. Out of nowhere, I’ll suddenly see it in my mind, as if it’s happening again—the sound of the crash, my husband slumped over. I don’t want to think about it, but the pictures just come.

Since then I’ve pulled away from people. I used to go to church groups and meet friends for lunch; now I mostly stay home, make excuses not to go out. I keep thinking, “If I’d insisted we leave earlier,” or “If I’d driven instead,” maybe he’d still be here. I go over it again and again, blaming myself.

I feel on edge all the time, like something bad is about to happen. Little things—a door slamming, a car horn—make my heart race and my hands shake, and it takes a long time to settle down. My head feels foggy a lot; I lose track of what I was doing, can’t focus on my books or even follow a TV show. That kind of trouble concentrating really only started after the accident.
D018-D001_h001.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

D018-D001_h002.question:
It started about eight months ago, after that scaffolding collapse at the construction site. Since then it’s like my whole system is on edge. If I hear a loud clang or someone walks up behind me quickly, I jump out of my skin. Even just seeing a building under renovation on the street can set me off—my chest tightens, my mind goes straight back to that day, and I feel this wave of panic that can last for hours.

I’ve pulled back from a lot of things I used to enjoy. I barely sketch for fun anymore, and I stopped going climbing with friends. Most nights I sit at home, just kind of numb but tense at the same time. I keep replaying what happened and thinking, “If I’d double-checked that detail, maybe no one would’ve been hurt.” That thought is constant.

Since the accident I also can’t focus the way I used to. I misplace my keys, forget where I saved project files, reread the same email three times. This wasn’t an issue earlier in my life; it really started only after the accident. And underneath everything there’s this steady, wired fear, like I’m waiting for something bad to happen again.
D018-D001_h002.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

D018-D001_h003.question:
It started a little over a year ago, after the break‑in at the museum. Before that, I was meticulous, could spend hours cataloging artifacts without losing focus. Since then, my head feels like it’s full of cotton a lot of the time. I’ll be midway through writing a label and suddenly I just… drift off or can’t hold a thought. That never used to happen.

Sometimes it’s much worse: I’ll hear a loud clang in the storage area, or someone drops a crate, and for a few seconds I’m not in the gallery anymore. I’m back in that night, hearing the glass shatter, feeling my body freeze. It’s so vivid it’s like it’s happening again. If a coworker brushes past me unexpectedly, I jump out of my skin; my whole body tenses before I even realize it’s just a touch.

I used to be proud of my exhibitions, but now I just feel numb about my work. People compliment a show and I think, “It doesn’t matter, I failed when it counted.” I keep replaying the night and blaming security, the board, even myself for not insisting on better protocols. There’s this constant, heavy shame, like I should have prevented everything that happened.
D018-D001_h003.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

D018-D001_h004.question:
It started about a year and a half ago, after that armed robbery at our office. Since then, my head just isn’t the same. I keep getting these images popping in, like I’m right back in the conference room with the gun in my face. It happens when I’m trying to work, or even when I’m putting my kids to bed. I don’t choose to think about it; it just crashes in.

I used to be very driven in my job, very proud of running HR smoothly. Now, even when I hit targets or complete a difficult restructuring, I feel flat, like, “So what?” It doesn’t matter. At the same time, I can’t stop going over how security failed that day, how management ignored my previous warnings; I keep replaying who’s to blame.

I’m on edge constantly—tense, jumpy, always waiting for something bad to happen. If someone taps me on the shoulder unexpectedly, I practically jump out of my skin. My focus has really gone downhill, but only since the robbery. Before that, I could sit through long meetings and read complex reports; now I lose track mid-sentence, even in simple conversations or watching TV.
D018-D001_h004.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

D018-D001_h005.question:
It’s been a little over two years since the accident on the highway, and I still feel like I’m living in its shadow.

Any time I hear screeching brakes, or even see a wreck on the side of the road, my whole body reacts before I can think—heart races, palms sweat, my chest tightens like I’m back there again. If someone grabs my shoulder from behind at the office, I jump out of my skin. I’ve snapped at coworkers for just brushing past me in a meeting.

I used to be really driven in my work. Now, even when I deliver a big project on time, I just feel…nothing. No pride, no sense of “good job.” It’s like it doesn’t matter. What I do think about a lot is how my ex-wife insisted we leave late that day—my head keeps spinning it so that if she hadn’t pushed the timing, maybe we wouldn’t have been on that stretch of road. I know that’s not entirely fair, but I can’t shake the anger; it’s always simmering, and I blow up over small things.

Since the accident, my concentration’s been shot. I didn’t have that problem as a kid or earlier in my career. Now I stare at emails, reread the same line over and over, can’t track conversations on client calls. Even picking what to eat for lunch or what shirt to wear can freeze me up for several minutes.
D018-D001_h005.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

D018-D001_h006.question:
It really started after my husband died three years ago. He collapsed in front of me at home, and everything after the ambulance arrived is kind of a blur. I know they worked on him, but I can’t piece most of it together, like my mind has walled that whole stretch of time off. I get fragments, then nothing.

These days, anything that reminds me of that night sets me off. If I hear a code called on TV or even a siren outside, I freeze and feel like I’m right back there, heart pounding, sometimes for hours. I do everything I can not to think about it—if my mind starts to go there, I shut it down, keep the TV on, do crossword puzzles, anything to avoid those memories.

What worries me is how much I’ve changed with people. My grandkids come over and I can’t seem to feel that warm, loving feeling I used to; it’s like I’m emotionally numb. I snap at them and at my daughter over little things, raise my voice, say harsh things I don’t mean. I also jump out of my skin if someone walks into a room behind me or moves quickly in my peripheral vision.

I never had trouble focusing as a child or during my nursing years. The difficulty concentrating on books or even a simple recipe really only started after my husband died and all this began.
D018-D001_h006.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D001_h007.question:
It started about a year and a half ago, after that break‑in at the open house. I can’t really piece together most of what happened inside the house that day; it’s like my brain just cut the middle out of the movie. I remember arriving, then the police, but the actual part in between is just… blank.

Since then I keep having these awful dreams. I wake up shaking and crying, seeing flashes of someone in the hallway, hearing banging doors. I avoid that neighborhood completely now. I make the junior agents handle showings in older houses, especially if they’re empty. Even normal things—like talking about security systems with clients—makes my chest tighten, so I change the subject.

At home I feel shut off from my husband and kids. I know I should feel close to them, but it’s like there’s a wall; I go through the motions, but I feel nothing.

I’m jumpy all the time—if a door slams or a car backfires, I physically flinch or almost duck. I snapped at my husband last month and shoved him when he came up behind me in the kitchen; I’ve slammed doors so hard I’ve cracked the frame.

My focus at work tanked only after all this. Before the break‑in, I could juggle listings and paperwork fine. Now I lose track mid‑conversation with clients, reread contracts over and over, and forget simple details, but that’s all been since that day.
D018-D001_h007.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D001_h008.question:

I can’t always see exactly what’s happening, but I wake up drenched in sweat, heart pounding. I’ve slammed doors and thrown the TV remote. And my concentration’s gone downhill only since the accident—I lose track of conversations or what I was doing mid-task, which was never a problem when I was still working.
D018-D001_h008.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)

D018-D001_h009.question:
It started about a year and a half ago, after that fall from the roof on the job. I hit the ground hard and I know there was a lot going on—sirens, people yelling—but big chunks of what actually happened are just…blank. My coworkers tell me details and it’s like they’re talking about someone else’s day, not mine. I can’t pull most of it up in my head no matter how hard I try.

Since then I’ve been having these awful dreams several nights a week. I’m back on that roof or falling, or I just wake up with my heart racing and this feeling like I’m in danger, even if I don’t remember the dream clearly. I try not to think about it at all—I change the subject, avoid driving past that job site, even skip certain kinds of work because anything that reminds me of it makes me feel sick.

I’ve also been way more jumpy. If someone taps me on the shoulder unexpectedly at work, I whip around and sometimes yell or swear before I even realize it’s my buddy. My wife says I snap at her and the kids over nothing. I used to be pretty easygoing and actually enjoyed stuff—taking the kids to the park, watching the game—but now even when something good happens, like getting a raise, I just feel flat, like I can’t access being happy.

My focus has gotten a lot worse too, but only since the accident. Before that, I could manage complex installs, read schematics, no problem. Now my mind drifts in the middle of wiring a panel, or I reread the same line on a work order five times. It’s not that I was always like this as a kid; this started after the fall.
D018-D001_h009.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)

D018-D001_h010.question:

I can remember parts of it so clearly—the sound of the metal, the yelling—but other parts are just blank, like someone cut pieces out of a movie. Since then, every so often, it’s like I’m right back there. I’m in the crane or even just at home, and suddenly I’m seeing it again, feeling it in my body, like it’s happening now. My wife has to shake me or call my name.

I’ve started doing anything I can to stay away from that site and folks who were there that day. Even driving past that area, or talking about similar jobs, I’ll just shut it down.

What’s really messing with me is I don’t feel happy anymore, even when I should—my kids’ birthdays, going fishing, stuff I used to love just feels flat. I snap at my wife and kids over nothing, yelling before I even realize it. If something loud startles me, my heart races and my hands shake for a long time after. And my focus at work went bad only after the accident—I never had trouble paying attention before all this happened.
D018-D001_h010.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)

D018-D001_h011.question:
It started about eight months ago, after that near-miss on the runway. Before that, I could lock onto a screen for hours without losing the thread. Now it’s like my brain keeps glitching—my eyes slide off the radar, I reread the same strip, and I miss things I never would’ve missed before. That only began after the incident.

When anything even vaguely reminds me of that night—the sound of a certain alarm, a similar weather pattern—I feel my heart pounding, palms sweating, like I’m right back there waiting for two blips to merge. Sometimes it’s just a thought popping up out of nowhere and my chest tightens immediately. I try to shove the memories away, push them down, keep myself too busy to think about it. If I start to picture it, I shut it off fast.

I’ve become really short-fused. Little things at work—someone talking too loud, a small delay—set me off, and I snap at colleagues. I don’t trust people like I used to; I keep thinking other controllers are careless, supervisors don’t really care, and that the whole mess was their fault for not backing me up. Honestly, I feel like most people are dangerous if you rely on them too much.
D018-D001_h011.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D001_h012.question:
It started about a year ago, after that destination wedding where the tent collapsed in the storm. No one died, but people were screaming, bleeding, I really thought someone was going to. Since then I’m not the same.

Sometimes, especially if there’s loud sudden noises or I’m under a big reception tent, it’s like I’m back there. I’m not just remembering it—I’m there: my heart’s racing, I can smell the wet fabric and hear people crying, and I lose track of where I actually am for a few seconds.

I’ve started dodging certain venues, outdoor tents, even avoiding calls with that couple and their families. I make excuses not to go to industry events where people might bring it up. I’ll cross the street to avoid construction sites or anything with flapping tarps.

My whole outlook has shifted. I keep thinking the world is basically unsafe, that something terrible could happen at any event I plan. I’m angry at the venue owner from that night and even at my boss for “pushing” that location—I replay it and blame them for not stopping it.

I’m on edge all the time now—snapping at my husband over nothing. And since that night, my focus has tanked. I used to juggle a dozen timelines; now I lose track of simple details. That concentration problem really only started after the accident.
D018-D001_h012.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D001_h013.question:
I’ve been out at the lighthouse about six years now, ever since that storm. The night that ship went down… I still see it, over and over, whether I want to or not. I’ll be checking the lamp or trying to sleep and suddenly I’m right back there—waves slamming the rocks, the radio cutting in and out, the flares I couldn’t reach in time. It just forces its way into my head.

Since then I can’t stand anything that reminds me of it. I avoid the cove where the wreck is, won’t go near the old radios or talk to the coast guard guys who were on duty that night. If someone brings it up in town, I just walk out.

My whole view of things has gone sour. I keep thinking the sea, the world in general, is just out to kill you and no one really cares. I blame the port authority, the shipping company, even the supervisor who cut our maintenance budget—I go over what they did wrong and it makes me furious.

I’ve started losing my temper physically. I’ve slammed doors hard enough to crack the frame, thrown tools across the room, once shoved a tech who wouldn’t drop the subject. I never used to be like that.

My concentration went downhill after that storm. Before then I could sit with charts for hours. Now my mind jumps back to that night, I lose my place in the logbook, forget simple steps in the maintenance checklist. It isn’t something I struggled with as a kid; it all started after the wreck.
D018-D001_h013.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D018-D001_h014.question:
